To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the relationship between reaction time and ratio is not always a linear function; rather it is modulated as a function of the type of stimuli and type of comparison.
the relationship between the discriminability of magnitudes and size ratios is not always linear.

the relationship between the discriminability of different magnitudes and their ratio is not always as suggested by the shared representation theory; rather, this relationship changes as a function the type of comparison, the type of stimuli and the familiarity with the compared magnitudes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the representation of magnitude in the human mind and the way it affects performance in different tasks.
the question: what is the nature of our representation of magnitude?
the building blocks of mathematical abilities, and the results shed new light on the nature of the mental number line.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Weber's law is not always valid for all types of magnitude comparisons.

the representation of magnitudes is not a single, rigid and universal mechanism, rather, it is an amalgamation of different mechanisms, which are activated as a function of the task demands and the type of stimulus.
the representation of number magnitude is not rigid and is modulated by different task demands and stimuli.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the magnitude system can be divided into two sub-systems, one for physical magnitudes and the other for symbolic magnitudes, and that these sub-systems are not necessarily identical.
different representations of magnitudes can be used to compare different stimuli, but the most efficient representation depends on the type of stimuli and the type of comparison.
the magnitude system is flexible and can accommodate different tasks, but it is still limited by its nature.
The main takeaway from our work is that
different magnitudes are not processed by the same representation.
the same stimuli can be represented by different mechanisms, depending on the task.
the relationship between size ratio and discriminability is not always linear and that the type of task and type of stimuli affect the relationship.
